verses.text: Now I declare to you, brothers, the Good News which I preached to you, which also you received, in which you also stand,
by which also you are saved, if you hold firmly the word which I preached to you — unless you believed in vain.
For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures,
that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,
and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.
Then he appeared to over five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, but some have also fallen asleep.
Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles,
and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also.
For I am the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God.
But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.
Whether then it is I or they, so we preach, and so you believed.
Now if Christ is preached, that he has been raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?
But if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ been raised.
If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain, and your faith also is in vain.
Yes, we are also found false witnesses of God, because we testified about God that he raised up Christ, whom he didn’t raise up, if it is so that the dead are not raised.
For if the dead aren’t raised, neither has Christ been raised.
If Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain; you are still in your sins.
Then they also who are fallen asleep in Christ have perished.
If we have only hoped in Christ in this life, we are of all men most pitiable.
But now Christ has been raised from the dead. He became the first fruits of those who are asleep.
For since death came by man, the resurrection of the dead also came by man.
For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.
But each in his own order: Christ the first fruits, then those who are Christ’s, at his coming.
Then the end comes, when he will deliver up the Kingdom to God, even the Father; when he will have abolished all rule and all authority and power.
For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet.
The last enemy that will be abolished is death.
For, “He put all things in subjection under his feet.”  But when he says, “All things are put in subjection”, it is evident that he is excepted who subjected all things to him.
When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son will also himself be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all.
Or else what will they do who are baptized for the dead? If the dead aren’t raised at all, why then are they baptized for the dead?
Why do we also stand in jeopardy every hour?
I affirm, by the boasting in you which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die daily.
If I fought with animals at Ephesus for human purposes, what does it profit me? If the dead are not raised, then “let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
Don’t be deceived! “Evil companionships corrupt good morals.”
Wake up righteously, and don’t sin, for some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.
But someone will say, “How are the dead raised?” and, “With what kind of body do they come?”
You foolish one, that which you yourself sow is not made alive unless it dies.
That which you sow, you don’t sow the body that will be, but a bare grain, maybe of wheat, or of some other kind.
But God gives it a body even as it pleased him, and to each seed a body of its own.
All flesh is not the same flesh, but there is one flesh of men, another flesh of animals, another of fish, and another of birds.
There are also celestial bodies, and terrestrial bodies; but the glory of the celestial differs from that of the terrestrial.
There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for one star differs from another star in glory.
So also is the resurrection of the dead. The body is sown perishable; it is raised imperishable.
It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.
It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body and there is also a spiritual body.
So also it is written, “The first man, Adam, became a living soul.”  The last Adam became a life-giving spirit.
However that which is spiritual isn’t first, but that which is natural, then that which is spiritual.
The first man is of the earth, made of dust. The second man is the Lord from heaven.
As is the one made of dust, such are those who are also made of dust; and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly.
As we have borne the image of those made of dust, let’s  also bear the image of the heavenly.
Now I say this, brothers,  that flesh and blood can’t inherit God’s Kingdom; neither does the perishable inherit imperishable.
Behold,  I tell you a mystery. We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed,
in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we will be changed.
For this perishable body must become imperishable, and this mortal must put on immortality.
But when this perishable body will have become imperishable, and this mortal will have put on immortality, then what is written will happen: “Death is swallowed up in victory.”
“Death, where is your sting? Hades,  where is your victory?”
The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.
But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.

footnotes.content: Paul opens with 'Now I declare'—a grandpa leaning forward to make sure I'm listening. He's not starting a new idea; he's anchoring us in Good News already preached and already held. What good news have you been *standing* in so long you almost forget you're standing?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Salvation is not a ticket stamped long ago—it requires holding *firmly* to the word preached. I think of a rope held taut; the grip matters as much as the rope. That 'if you believed in vain' warns gently: belief that drifts or weakens has already come loose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul delivers what he received—the heart of it: *Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures*. This is not Paul's invention but the tradition of the apostles, rooted in Israel's own hope. He hands it on as sacred trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Buried. Raised. On the third day. Not a spiritual vapor but a real, sequence-bound event. The body went into the earth; something real and embodied rose. The Scriptures had already written this—Isaiah 53, Psalm 16. God was keeping His word all along.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cephas first—Peter, the rock Jesus renamed, the one who denied Him thrice. That Jesus appears first to the very apostle who broke faith speaks volumes. Restoration comes before proclamation; the risen Lord finds you where you fell.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Five hundred witnesses, most still living when Paul writes. Not legend—not yet. Real people, many still around to confirm or refute. 'Some have fallen asleep' uses that gentle word for death, hinting at the resurrection to come even in the phrase.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: James—Jesus' own brother, skeptical until the resurrection (John 7:5). Then the risen Jesus appears to him, and James becomes a pillar of the Jerusalem church. Sometimes the skeptics in your own family need their own encounter with the risen One.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul calls himself 'the child born at the wrong time'—the abortion, the untimely one. He appeared to me also, he says. Not boasting, just fact: the same resurrected Jesus who met Peter, James, and five hundred, met Paul on the Damascus road and remade him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul won't let himself off the hook: 'I persecuted the assembly of God.' He's not hiding his past to claim apostolic standing. The very ones he hunted down are now his brothers and sisters. That's the kind of humility that earns trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A watershed verse: 'By the grace of God I am what I am.' Grace is not sentimental—it's transformative, giving him strength to work harder than all the apostles. Yet in the same breath he says 'not I, but the grace.' That paradox is the Christian life: maximum effort, zero pride.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Whether I or they, so we preach. Paul is saying: the message is unified. He and the other apostles are not in competition—they preach one Christ. And the Corinthians believed that one word. Unity in witness makes the testimony ring true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The logical knot: Christ is preached as raised—that's the gospel itself. Yet some among you say no resurrection exists. If the head rose but the body cannot rise, what does that do to hope? Paul is about to untie this knot.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The domino falls: no resurrection of the dead means Christ wasn't raised either. Paul won't let skepticism hide in half-measures. If you deny the general resurrection, you must deny His—and that collapses everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Preaching is hollow. Faith is hollow. The message becomes words without power, a hope without footing. Paul won't soften this: deny the resurrection and you've cut the nerve of the gospel itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: False witnesses—the apostles would be liars if they testified God raised Jesus and He didn't. Paul stakes his integrity on the fact of the resurrection. No wiggle room. That kind of certainty comes only from having seen Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The logic circles back: if the dead can't rise, Christ couldn't have risen. Paul drives home the consequence without apology. Either death is not the end for anyone, or it is—you can't have it both ways.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Without His resurrection, your faith is vain and you're *still in your sins*. The weight of that sits heavy: every sin unforgiven, every guilt unredeemed. This is not abstract theology—this is your actual standing before God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Those who died believing in a risen Christ? Without the resurrection, they have perished utterly. No second thought, no hope beyond the grave. For Paul, this is unthinkable—and the very thing that should wake Corinth up.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Most pitiable of all men.' To hope in Christ only for this life is to aim at a target that vanishes. Sickness, betrayal, loss—they all win in the end if death is final. But that's not the hope Paul preaches.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But now—the great pivot. Christ *has been* raised. Not will be; already is. 'First fruits' echoes Leviticus: the first sheaf of harvest pledges what follows. His resurrection is the guarantee of ours.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Death entered through one man, Adam—all die because all inherit his nature and his fall. Resurrection comes through one man, Jesus—by His life we are made alive. The parallel is exact and complete.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In Adam all die; in Christ all will be made alive. Not some—*all*. The scope of His victory is as wide as the scope of death itself. Every person Adam, every person Christ touches will rise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Each in his own order: Christ first, then those who are His at His coming. Not chaos but order, like a harvest in stages. First the grain appears, then the ear, then the full corn in the ear. Christ is first; we follow in appointed time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The end comes. The Kingdom handed over to the Father. All rule and authority abolished. This is not the world's ending but its coronation—Jesus returning power to God, and with it, the removal of every opposing force.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He must reign until all enemies are under His feet. Not waiting, not passive—He's actively reigning, actively subduing opposition. Psalm 110 wrote this long ago. The script was already written.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The last enemy that will be abolished is death. Paul singles it out—of all the forces Christ must overcome, death comes last. When death is gone, every other enemy is already behind us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul quotes Psalm 8: 'He put all things in subjection under his feet'—spoken of humanity in the psalm, now fulfilled in the risen Christ. Yet one exception: the Father who subjected all things. The hierarchy remains: Christ under God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Son subjects Himself to the Father, and God becomes all in all. This is not degradation but the deepest harmony—Son and Father in perfect unity, all things reconciled, nothing left divided or at odds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Baptized for the dead—an odd practice, its meaning debated even then. Paul uses it to argue: why practice it at all if the dead won't rise? The very fact that some do it shows belief in resurrection is woven into church life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Why stand in jeopardy every hour? Paul reminds them he and the apostles are risking their lives. This is not armchair philosophy. Belief in the resurrection costs them daily danger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'I die daily'—by the boasting in you which I have in Christ. Paul faces death constantly and finds joy in the Corinthians' faith. His daily dying isn't despair; it's the rhythm of dying to self so Christ can live.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If I fought with animals at Ephesus—whether literal or metaphorical, Paul endured brutal opposition. He quotes Isaiah 22:13: 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.' That's the pagan's logic. But only *if* the dead aren't raised.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Evil companionships corrupt good morals—a warning from Greek playwright Menander, cited as true. Bad company has a gravity that pulls believers down. Resurrection hope is fragile if you're surrounded by those who deny it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wake up righteously and don't sin. Some have no knowledge of God—Paul isn't excusing them but diagnosing the problem. Ignorance of resurrection naturally leads to moral drift. Right thinking leads to right living.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The natural objection: How are the dead raised, and in what body? Paul is not surprised by the question. He's been waiting for it. Now he'll answer with patience and picture.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You foolish one—Paul is blunt but not unkind. Plant a seed and it doesn't live unless it dies. You already know resurrection in nature every spring. The risen body follows the pattern God wrote into creation itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You sow a bare grain—wheat or something else. Not the full-grown plant, just the seed. Yet from that tiny thing, life emerges. The body we sow is nothing like the body we reap, yet it's continuity, not escape.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God gives it a body as He pleased—each seed gets its own kind of body. If the Creator is so generous with corn and beans, why doubt He'll give us resurrection bodies suited to His glory?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All flesh is not the same—human, animal, fish, bird. God loves variety. The resurrection body won't be some ghost or uniform substance but tailored, specific, glorified *you*.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Celestial and terrestrial bodies—sun, moon, earth, sky. Each has its own glory, its own kind of beauty. The risen body is celestial, not terrestrial, yet still a body—real, visible, glorious.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One glory of the sun, another of the moon, another of the stars—each star differs from another in glory. The point sings: diversity in beauty, hierarchy in splendor. The resurrection itself will show such variety.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: So also is the resurrection of the dead—the pivot. All that Paul has said about seeds and stars and different flesh now applies directly. Sown perishable; raised imperishable. The transition is complete; the principle proven from nature.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sown in dishonor—the grave, decay, corruption. Raised in glory. Sown in weakness—death conquers the flesh. Raised in power—no weakness, no shadow remains. The contrast is absolute.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sown a natural body; raised a spiritual body. Not disembodied but transformed—a body fit for the Spirit, ruled by the Spirit instead of by instinct and decay. Real and glorified.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The first man, Adam, became a living soul—quoted from Genesis 2. The last Adam became a life-giving spirit. Jesus does what Adam could not: He imparts life, not just receives it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The natural is first, then the spiritual. We begin as Adam did—flesh-bound, earthly. We end in Christ—spirit-filled, transformed. The order is fixed: first perishable, then imperishable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The first man is of the earth, made of dust. The second man is the Lord from heaven. Not two competitors but two heads, two Adams: one earthly, one heavenly. We trace our resurrection through the second.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As is the one made of dust, such are those made of dust—we bear Adam's image, his nature, his mortality. As is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly—we shall bear Christ's image, His nature, His immortality.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: We have borne the image of the dusty; let's also bear the image of the heavenly. Not 'someday will'—Paul uses the hortative: it's already our calling. We're becoming what we shall be.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Flesh and blood can't inherit God's Kingdom—not because the body is evil, but because flesh and blood as they are now—perishable, mortal—can't survive God's presence. Transformation is not optional but necessary.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Behold, I tell you a mystery. Paul leans in close. Not all will sleep, but all will be changed—the living and the dead, all of us transformed in an instant. It's mystery, yes, but it's one Paul stakes his apostolic word on.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. Not slowly, not gradually—suddenly, like lightning. The trumpet sounds and the dead rise imperishable, the living transformed, all in that instant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This perishable must become imperishable; this mortal must put on immortality. What *must* happen will happen. The necessity is not burden but promise—death itself is temporary.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Death is swallowed up in victory—Paul quotes Isaiah 25:8. At that moment the ancient prophecy is fulfilled. Death, the last enemy, is not destroyed or managed but utterly swallowed, consumed by Jesus' triumph.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory? Paul turns taunt into song. He's quoting Hosea 13:14, throwing death's own weapons back at it. The risen Lord has silenced both.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sting of death is sin; the power of sin is the law. Sin makes death terrible. The law exposes sin. But Christ has paid sin's debt and fulfilled the law—so death's sting is drawn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in 'Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory.' In every loss, every ache, every goodbye—we still say thanks, because the victory is Christ's and therefore ours. As of 2026-10, I'm grateful that death is already defeated, even when it still hurts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord's work. Your labor is not in vain in the Lord. Paul ends not with escape but with work—faithful, growing, anchored. The resurrection calls us not to passivity but to perseverance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
